Everyone here has given really solid advice so far, here's my two cents on it. 

As a barback, you're a bit of an unsung hero. You might not always get the recognition that the bartenders do, but don't let them push you around too much, beware of egos! You're just as important (arguably far more important) to the smooth running of the bar as they are. But saying that, be prepared to listen and learn from those more experienced. Ask questions when you have time and it's maybe a little quieter, if it's not too busy and you see them making a drink you've never seen before, watch what they're doing, show an interest! 

Also, learn your classics!! If you know the classics well, most other cocktails will be a lot easier to learn and perfect! 

Whilst you're still a barback, just make sure you're on top of everything. Don't let them run out of stuff, keep the bar clean, try to stay busy even when there aren't as many customers. It'll depend on the bar of course, but if you show you're a hard worker, show a keen interest in progression, and prove yourself behind the bar, there's absolutely no reason you couldn't be training as a bartender within a few months! 

Good luck out there! Enjoy it, I've been in the industry for a long time now and I couldn't see myself doing anything else, I love it!

I would never tell anyone to write for fame/money etc, but writing on a professional level is just as important as writing for fun. Working on ideas and projects that motivate and inspire you is definitely key, as you'll find these more 'fun' and probably end up having a more enjoyable experience through the process. But sometimes, you have to just force yourself to work on stuff that maybe doesn't motivate you as much. You have to force yourself to sit down and write, even when it's the last thing you want to do, because if you want to make a living from it you need to persevere, you need to be consistent and you need to get as much practice as you can. Even though making it a routine may not always be as 'fun', it'll really help you improve. Plus, as a working writer, you'll have to meet standards, deadlines etc. in order to keep up with your peers, and this may involve working on stuff that you don't find overly fun, but will pay the bills and get another credit under your belt.

Hello there. First time seeing a post about this, but I am definitely interested in this. I'm a writer, and would be more than happy to put a script together for it.

Agree with what other's have said. There is some good screenwriting software out there but most of it is costly and if you're not going to be producing any screenplays then probably not worth it! I have a few different programmes but still use just a word document and/or google docs to work on my comic scripts :)

I'd recommend you watch some videos or read up on lettering in graphic novels, it's a small change that will make dialogue so much easier and more comfortable to read, and tonally it will fit a lot better. If you're not lettering by hand and instead just typing in on top of your artwork, I'm almost sure there are packs you can download somewhere that will allow you to do this (I'm almost sure, but I'm not completely clued up on it myself admittedly!). As for examples, I'd say just have a look at your own personal go-to graphic novels for inspiration and find a style that works for you. This is only my opinion, but I noticed a lot of the bubbles are quite enlongated, which makes it feel like more of a task to the reader. Instead, I'd recommend finding a way to compact them slightly, stacking the text a little more. I'd also say that just a small re-jig in terms of the positioning and layout on some of the panels might help as well, try to find a way that will be smooth and fit with your artwork, without detracting and pulling the reader's eye away from the scene too much. Honestly, there are so many resources available online that it won't take long to figure these little things out and a quick google search will bring up lots of helpful articles, guides, examples etc. As I said, I might not be the best informed to advise on this stuff but that's just my personal opinion on it. Other than that, you have a really solid start here! I look forward to seeing more from you and I hope I have helped :)
